body_markdown:
A fraudster who used dating apps to build relationships with women before exploiting their trust has been jailed after deceiving victims out of almost £80,000.


Joseph Gibson, 35, created an elaborate web of lies about his health, wealth and personal history. He claimed to have cancer, told victims he had suffered serious injuries while serving in the Royal Navy, and presented himself as a hugely successful businessman with access to luxury homes, yachts and other expensive possessions.


Instead, prosecutors said the stories were part of a calculated scheme designed to persuade people to give him money.


Gibson, from Ruthin Wells, pleaded guilty to four charges of fraud by false representation relating to offences committed between July 2020 and October 2021. He was sentenced to three years and two months in prison at Bristol Crown Court.


He has also promised to repay his victims using approximately £40,000 in savings.


## A carefully constructed deception


Gibson met two of his victims through Tinder. He presented himself as a wealthy and successful man and, in at least one case, convinced his victim that they were in a genuine romantic relationship.


His claims about his finances were extraordinary. He told victims that he was worth hundreds of millions of pounds, claimed to own or have access to luxury properties and boats, and spoke about investments and business opportunities.


At the same time, he used a very different story when asking for money.


Gibson repeatedly claimed that he had cancer and needed funds for medical treatment. He sent photographs that appeared to show him in hospital, including images of himself lying in a hospital bed and another showing what appeared to be a blood catheter in his wrist.


Messages released by Avon and Somerset Police show how he reinforced the story.


In one message, he told a victim that he believed his cancer had returned. He later claimed that doctors had confirmed the diagnosis and wanted him to begin radiotherapy.


The victim believed the claims and sent him money.


The deception had a devastating financial impact. One woman, a Devon-based businesswoman, lost more than £5,200 over a period of four months. At one point, she was left with just 93 pence in her bank account.


She had initially sent Gibson £100 after he told her that he had cancer and was experiencing financial pressure. He subsequently persuaded her to provide more money, claiming that he was using it to purchase stock for her retail business.


## Victims were persuaded to borrow money


Another woman Gibson met on Tinder was drawn into an even longer-running deception.


He allegedly told her that he was receiving treatment at University College London Hospital and claimed that he had suffered radiation damage while serving in the Royal Navy. He also said that he had been "blown up by an IED".


He told the woman that his cancer had returned and that he urgently needed money for private treatment.


Believing that she was helping someone she was romantically involved with, she took out a £4,000 loan.


The financial losses continued as Gibson maintained the appearance of being wealthy. He reportedly spoke about buying a yacht in Corfu for around £6 million and claimed to have extensive property interests.


The victim eventually lost more than £21,000 after taking out personal loans and accumulating credit card debt.


In a victim impact statement, she described the consequences in deeply personal terms, saying the fraud had broken her as a person and turned her life upside down.


## Luxury claims helped maintain the illusion


Gibson's alleged stories were not limited to his health.


He told victims that he had climbed Mount Everest and claimed to own boats, property in Dubai and a home in Mayfair. He also spoke about having a yacht in Monaco and being able to fly a helicopter.


On one occasion, while claiming to be in hospital, he asked a victim to buy him clothes and have them delivered to the hospital. When asked about his spending limit, he claimed that he was valued at £440 million.


In another message, he referred to Sandbanks in Dorset as his retreat and claimed to own a house and 21 rented properties there.


These extravagant claims appear to have helped reinforce the impression that he was financially secure, making his requests for money appear temporary or believable.


## Other victims were targeted through investment claims


Two further victims were also caught up in Gibson's lies.


A relative of one of the women was persuaded to take out loans and provide money for investment opportunities that prosecutors said were bogus. She lost more than £18,000.


Another victim was a former superyacht captain who had been persuaded by Gibson's claims about his interest in sailing and boats. He handed over more than £25,000 for what he believed was an investment in Gibson's business.


The man later described Gibson as a dangerous con artist who would not stop taking money from people.


The cases demonstrate how fraud can rely on more than one form of manipulation. Romantic trust, apparent financial success, fabricated medical emergencies and promises of investment can all be combined to create a convincing story.


## The wider warning about romance fraud


The case also highlights the risks associated with romance fraud, in which criminals develop relationships with victims before asking for money or financial assistance.


Fraudsters may spend weeks or months building trust. They can create detailed identities, use photographs and messages to support false claims, and adapt their stories when victims begin to ask questions.


Medical emergencies can be particularly powerful because they create urgency and make victims feel that refusing to help could have serious consequences.


The apparent wealth Gibson displayed created another contradiction that victims may have struggled to reconcile. A person claiming to be extremely wealthy should not ordinarily need relatively small sums for everyday expenses. However, once trust has been established, such inconsistencies can be explained away.


For anyone meeting a new romantic partner online, requests for money should therefore be treated with caution, particularly when they are accompanied by urgent medical, business or travel-related explanations.


It is also important to remember that genuine relationships should not require someone to take out loans, use credit cards or hand over their savings to prove their affection.


Gibson's case shows how sophisticated deception can become when emotional manipulation is combined with financial fraud. His claims about cancer and extraordinary wealth were allegedly designed to serve the same purpose: convincing victims that the person they trusted was genuine.


Instead, the court heard that those stories helped him take almost £80,000 from four people.


His imprisonment provides a measure of accountability, while his promise to repay around £40,000 may offer some financial redress. But the impact on his victims extends beyond the money they lost.


The case is a reminder that fraud can leave lasting emotional damage, particularly when the deception comes from someone a victim believed was a romantic partner or trusted associate.
